text: Hi, everyone.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This talk will be about how to run agents reliably in production.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It will not be about the eFile part, but it will be about all the other things you need to get going in order to run agents resiliently.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the infrastructure layer, basically.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I want to set the scene with this quote of Andrej Carpathy of last week.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It describes that the way we interact with agents and LLMs has been evolving in three waves.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The first wave was an LLM being something like a website where we go to, we ask it a question, it thinks for a few seconds and then gives us a response.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The second wave was going towards agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It was an app that we downloaded to our computer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It has some tools at its disposal, and it can do some work with our interaction.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, the third wave will be going more and more towards persistent and asynchronous entities, so agents being long-running processes in our infrastructure with access to tools and other agents around the organization and context.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so as our use cases are evolving more and more from single agents to agentic platforms that connect parts around the organization, our infrastructure layer should also evolve with that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So when we look at the types of tools that are currently out there to implement agents, a lot of innovation has been done on sites such as agent SDKs and memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And ancient SEKs are really cool to implement POCs and get started quickly, but they don't necessarily help with connecting the distributed bits around an organization.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And if you want to implement more complex agentic systems, you actually need all of those things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So that is the layer that you see below here, where you have to deploy extra infrastructure, you need to write things like retry logic, recovery logic, and all of that is actually pretty complex to get right, but completely necessary to run long-running stateful and distributed processes in production.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So today I want to talk about an open source framework called Restate.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And you can see it a bit as a flexible, durable foundation that lets you build any backend.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So it's not specific for agents, but as agents are also just a type of a backend, it also works well for them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The ideas behind ReState come from Apache Flink, which is a popular distributed stream processing engine, and also from some of the ex-architects behind Metascore Event Infra.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what are the ingredients in ReState?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Basically four parts.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First of all, it makes sure that a single run of an agent is resilient.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is called durable execution in the industry.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Think about things like when an agent runs for a week and then crashes, we want to be able to bring it back and let it continue exactly at the point where it failed.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We don't want it to start over from the beginning.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Another area here is running many concurrent sessions in parallel.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Imagine running thousands of concurrent agent sessions at the same time and needing to make sure that state is always consistent and that different agents don't interfere with each other.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then going more towards things like communication between agents, between agents and MCP servers and other tools, and finally also control, making sure that when an agent, for example, is doing something you don't want it to continue or when it's stuck, being able to actually cancel or kill the execution.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So, the way that you can think of it is as follows.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Restate is basically a server which runs in front of your agent service, so as a separate component.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It sits there a bit like a message broker or a proxy.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And when there's a request for your agent, Restate proxies the request to the service and pushes it to the service, basically.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And from that moment, there's a connection, open connection between Restate and the agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that connection will basically be a bit like a lifeline for the agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So as the agent is doing stuff, it sends events over to Restate, and Restate will use that journal of events to recover the process after a failure.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So from a slightly higher level explanation, you could say that it's turning a normal function in your application into something that is long-running, durable, and stateful, without having to do a lot of the complex things you otherwise need to do for this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: LLM call, and the way I made it durable is by wrapping it in restate.run.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what happens is by doing these durable steps, if this fails somewhere here, two hours or two months later, it will recover to exactly that point.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So that's the idea of durable execution.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You're always able to recover a process to where it was.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can also use that for other things, not necessarily for failure recovery.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For example, imagine we want to ask a human to approve something, and this approval might take weeks or a month.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This process needs to be able to survive restarts and redeploys over those kind of long periods of time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so with durable execution you can actually also suspend a function and bring it back when it's able to make progress.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So in the case of a human approval what we do here is basically we create a durable promise which lives in that journal a bit like a suspension point.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then we ask
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So if it's running on serverless, this is not using execution time on our functions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what we see here is a bit like a workflow.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's a set of steps that get executed durable.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But when we think about agents and also the way that Carpathie described it in the tweet, it's more like a persistent stateful entity that lives for a longer period of time, that has some memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So a workflow is not the nicest way to model this kind of thing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the way that we can model this in Restate is by using something called a virtual object.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So imagine in the use case that I'm showing this Slack research agent, imagine that I don't want to wait for 10 minutes to give it some follow-up context or maybe I think about something else that I should have told it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I want to actually be able to interact with it, not wait till that research is finished before I can send a follow-up.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so this is basically what a virtual object in restate is.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's a bit like a stateful actor.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It has a unique ID, for example, a session ID.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It has some key value states that is isolated for that specific session that you can write to.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Imagine, for example, your history of messages.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And it also has like a set of handlers that can execute durable functions for this session.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So here, the way I implemented this use case that I mentioned of interacting with a running process is as follows.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is a session controller.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Again, it has like this restate object context at its disposal to do things in a recoverable way.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It can write to the session store.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Here I'm retrieving the chat history.

text: And one thing that's interesting there is that in order to run these kind of sessions in very high parallelized ways, so thousands of sessions at the same time, we need to make sure that agents do not interfere with each other.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Imagine I'm sending two messages on Slack and now two agents are actually overwriting each other's session state.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: To prevent that, this will guarantee that only one execution is running at a time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So a second execution will be queued behind the current one.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then, let's have a look at how we implement this, like interacting with another execution.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So, an execution in Reset has a unique identifier, and you can use that identifier to connect to it from other processes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For example, to retrieve the output, but also to cancel it, or maybe to signal it, being injecting a bit of state into an already running agent loop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so this is a very flexible type of capabilities that you can do to implement things like, for example, signaling an already ongoing agent loop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what we do here is if there is a current execution ongoing, then we will ask an LLM, is this something that is relevant for the current agent loop?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And so this goes a little bit further than workflows.

text: Let's go back to the slides to have a little more of an idea of how this thing is actually implemented on the inside because it's actually a pretty interesting design or architecture.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the way it's implemented is basically by having an event-driven distributed log implementation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So inside the box you basically on one side have the clients, on the other side the services, and inside the box is a log which persists all those journal events and an event loop.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that event loop basically gets the events from the service
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Based on what the event is, it either persists some state in the embedded state store, or it sets a timer, or it sends a request to another agent, and by doing that you basically have a durable foundation for whatever an application is doing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The design of this distributed log is heavily inspired by the way that the core event infralayer at Meta works.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's basically like an iteration on top of that, and some of those architects now have designed that for restates as a more generic solution that is available in open source.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: There are two important things related to this architecture that make it interesting.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The first one is that it works as a push model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So, whereas most workflow orchestrators actually pull for new tasks, pull from the workflow server, Restate actually
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: pushes the invocations.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the benefit you get from that is that it has a much lower latency.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So you can use these kind of workflow guarantees in functions around your application and have like a latency of, for example, 45 milliseconds p99 for like a 10-step workflow.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Pushing invocations also works very well for serverless because they require you to basically send the request and wake up the function.
speaker: SPEAKER_00
